extracted.intended_audience: landscape and marine painters; serious art students and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for depicting water (lakes, rivers, waterfalls, seas) in painting, emphasizing optical truth, handling of reflections, color, brushwork, and expressive character. Applicable to artists producing realistic or expressive water in oil/watercolor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful reflections (no wilful invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflections should accord with optical truth and not be wilfully invented to disguise weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author criticizes painters (e.g., Canaletto, Vandevelde) who place reflections or ripples incorrectly to cheat distance—calling such devices 'wilful and inexcusable violation of truth' born of the painter's consciousness of weakness. Do not use invented reflections to supply 'some means of expressing retirement of surface' when you lack knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve liquidity of the sea
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not paint the sea as a walkable or billiard-table-like extent; maintain its liquidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better to feel a want of extent in the sea than to give an extent 'which we might walk upon or play at billiards upon.' Avoid gray horizontal lines that make the surface look flat and solid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct relation of sky vs object reflections with distance
rubrics_metrics.description: As water retires, it should show more sky reflection and less reflection of nearer objects; distant water should become an even field of sky-color without object reflections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canaletto is faulted for the reverse: he 'displays more and more of the reflection of objects, and less and less of the sky' as the canal recedes. Follow optical rules: distant water, especially hundreds of yards away, tends toward uniform sky-color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monotonous, uniform rippling
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not cover the whole water surface with one monotonous ripple or repeating device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of Canaletto's 'one monotonous ripple' of sea-green covered with numerous white concave touches—an easy device that sacrifices truthful variety and subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every ripple is a mirror—capture mixed reflected tints
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual waves act as mirrors and pick up the hues of sky, boats, marble, seaweed, etc.; therefore waves should carry mixed, transparent color rather than an opaque dead green.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canaletto's thousand ripples contradict 'the truths of color' by presenting an opaque dead green. Aim for transparent emerald hues that mingle with reflected tints without overpowering them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conventionalism; study real marine effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not tolerate mechanical or conventional water-painting; marine effects should be carefully studied from nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venetian and Florentine masters often use broad extents of color but neglect detailed aqueous study. The author urges close observation of real sea behavior rather than reliance on inherited conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express true motion and form of waves and foam
rubrics_metrics.description: Waves should be shown falling, plunging, tossing, crashing; foam should fly and flash, not sit astride or curl like shavings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of Vandevelde: 'Foam appears ... to curdle and cream on the wave sides and to fly, flashing from their crests, and not to be set astride upon them like a peruke.' Avoid static or artificial foam shapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose expressive moment (avoid insipid instant selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select moments that reveal character and power; do not habitually pick the most insipid or characterless instant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claude's seas are noted as 'selections of the particular moment when the sea is most insipid and characterless.' Prefer moments that show the subject's force and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied and studied grays (melodies of quiet color)
rubrics_metrics.description: When painting scenes dominated by gray (storms, desolation), employ studied, varied grays with subtle inflections (greens, browns, yellows) to sustain interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fielding's admirable aim at 'character' can fail without 'studied melodies of quiet color.' The eye, deprived of bright points, examines grays mercilessly—so grays must be rich, variable, and melodious (examples: Turner's Land's End, Lowestoffe, Snowstorm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on chiaroscuro tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not depend on dark skies, driving spray, or dramatic chiaroscuro to hide shortcomings in form or color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stanfield is praised for painting sea in open daylight with 'nothing more than chaste and unexaggerated local color'—he 'fears no difficulty' and does not need dark skies to gain relief. Use local color and form rather than theatrical concealment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use decisive, swift execution for drawing running water
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid, decisive brushwork captures the true curves and instantaneous character of torrents and falls better than slow finish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: J. D. Harding praised: 'in a rapid touch the hand naturally falls into the very curve of projection which is the absolute truth.' Slow finish risks loss of precision of curve and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render waterfalls' mist and spray with delicacy and substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture the veils of spray and mist delicately, but balance them with definite grays and substance in parts not affected by spray.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nesfield is commended for 'management of the changeful veil of spray or mist' and 'unequalled in color,' but criticized for sometimes losing 'simplicity and dignity' and needing 'more definite and prevalent grays' and 'a little more substance to parts of his picture unaffected by spray.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish surface impression from depth (surface vs morbid clearness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid rendering reflections so clearly that they suggest plunging into depth; preserve the sense of surface by making reflections vague in form while keeping color and light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The difficulty: giving surface is near impossible if reflections are painted with the clearness natural to distant objects—this produces 'morbidly clear' water. Turner's approach: make reflections 'evidently reflections of something definite and determined; but yet ... uncertain and inexplicable' so the eye rests on the surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paint margin reflections distinctly, distant reflections vaguer
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflections of margin objects (close to the observer) should be clear and distinct; reflections of distant objects must be vague and indistinct to maintain surface-focus effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author: 'the ordinary effect of water is only to be rendered by giving the reflections of the margin clear and distinct ... but the moment we touch the reflection of distant objects ... we must become vague and uncertain in drawing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulate ocular focus limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose and render water with awareness that the eye cannot simultaneously focus on surface detail and deep reflections; painting must mimic this selective focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by duckweed experiment: you can either see the surface leaves or the reflection, not both. Use this physiological fact to decide which elements to draw sharply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim at character and emotional impact, not only correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond technical truth, strive to make the viewer feel the character (desolation, terror, repose) of the water—truth must be allied with feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fielding's 'high aim at character' is praised; Stanfield is great in knowledge but 'wanting in what we have just been praising in Fielding--impressiveness.' The best works combine technical truth with affective power (Turner exemplified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local color and transparency over dead gray or cold hues
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain local color and transparency in water; avoid dead, cold grays that appear as a positive hue of water and rob it of depth/character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harding's fault: 'a bad gray... too dead and cold' in bright, unreflected water. Fielding's sea was once right in green/gray but later 'verged more and more on the purple and black' with unhappy results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid perpetual repetition of the same idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety in conception is necessary; repeating identical compositions or effects weakens the artist's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fielding is criticized: 'in all his life, can only be considered as having produced _one_ sea picture. The others are duplicates.' Seek variety of approach and subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment as a compositional tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn how to conceal certain elements (reserve, omission) to increase impressiveness and affect the viewer more strongly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author advises Stanfield to 'learn how to conceal'—concealment can make a work more affecting rather than merely clever or exhaustive in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use observation of diverse natural situations as models
rubrics_metrics.description: Study a range of real water conditions—calm lakes, mountain tarns, cataracts, coasts in bright daylight—to build a complete repertoire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author lists specialists: Fielding (quiet lakes), Robson (deep calm water), De Wint (lowland river), Nesfield (cataract), Harding (torrent), Stanfield (open ocean). Arrange these studies to 'comprise a complete history' of water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect scale in ripple size diminution
rubrics_metrics.description: Ripples should geometrically diminish in size with distance so that far-off water becomes an even field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canaletto 'very geometrically diminishes the size of his ripples' but fails in color/reflection decisions; the rule is: ripples diminish in scale with distance and ultimately produce an apparently smooth surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using white concave touches as cheap distance device
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on repetitive white concave touches to fake surface retirement across large fields of water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author condemns white touches used by Canaletto as occupying space 'without any troublesome necessity for knowledge or invention'—they are an easy escape for awkward hands and deceive the public but violate truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give different parts of water appropriate weight/substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance luminous, delicate passages (spray, mist, foam) with substantial, definite treatment of other areas so the composition has gravitas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nesfield is commended for delicate color but warned that without 'more definite and prevalent grays' and 'a little more substance' in unaffected parts, the picture lacks balance between lustre and gloom.
